LESSONS.title: Classes and objects
LESSONS.goal: Make objects from a class and read their values
summary: A class is a blueprint; an object is the real thing
Each call to Cat() makes one new object
A dot reads and sets an object's values

cards.say: A class is a blueprint, and an object is a real thing built from that blueprint. class Cat is a cat blueprint. Call Cat() and you get one cat (an object), and a dot reads its values.
cards.code:
class Cat:
    kind = "cat"
c = Cat()
print(c.kind)

cards.say: One blueprint can build many things. Each object can hold its own values, so even though a and b are both Cats, they have different names.
cards.code:
class Cat:
    kind = "cat"
a = Cat()
b = Cat()
a.name = "Nabi"
b.name = "Momo"
print(a.name, b.name)

items.q: Which one is the blueprint?
items.explain: class Cat is the blueprint. c = Cat() is the real thing built from that blueprint, in other words, an object.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
class Cat:
    kind = "cat"
c = Cat()
print(c.kind)
items.explain: c is an object made from Cat, so it can read the kind written in the blueprint with a dot.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
class Cat:
    kind = "cat"
a = Cat()
b = Cat()
a.name = "Nabi"
b.name = "Momo"
print(a.name)
items.explain: a and b are different things built from the same blueprint. The value put into a.name sticks to a only.

items.q: Fill in the blank to make an object so cat is printed.
items.code:
class Cat:
    kind = "cat"
c = ___()
print(c.kind)
items.explain: Call the blueprint's name, Cat, with parentheses. Lowercase cat is a name that doesn't exist, so NameError, and class is a reserved word, so SyntaxError.

items.q: Put the lines in order: the blueprint first, then the object.
items.explain: The blueprint has to exist before Cat() can build anything. And only once it's built can you read c.kind.

items.task: Read a name with input() (leave the parentheses empty) into name. Make class Cat with kind = "cat", make c with Cat(), and put name into c.name. Print it like “Nabi (cat)”. For Nabi: Nabi (cat)
hints: The output changes with the name you enter. What should it print for Momo?
An object is a thing built from a blueprint (class). You can put values into an object with a dot.
Make c with Cat(), put the entered name into c.name, then take out c.name and c.kind and print them.

name = input()
c = ___()
c.name = name
(print c.name and c.kind with the parentheses)
items.solution:
class Cat:
    kind = "cat"
name = input()
c = Cat()
c.name = name
print(c.name, "(" + c.kind + ")")
items.explain: There's one blueprint, but each input makes an object with a different name. The name sticks to the object, and kind comes from the blueprint.

items.q: What happens when you call Cat() twice?
options: Both point to the same object
items.explain: Every call builds one new thing from the blueprint. The blueprint itself stays as one.

LESSONS.title: __init__ and attributes
LESSONS.goal: Use __init__ to give an object values as it's born
summary: __init__ runs when an object is made
self is the very object being made
self.name = value attaches an attribute
Put objects in a list and loop with for

cards.say: Setting a name on every object by hand gets tiring. __init__ runs by itself the moment an object is made. Here, self is the very thing being made right now.
Call Cat("Nabi") and "Nabi" goes into name. Python fills in self for you, so you don't write it when calling. Each object has its own self.name.
cards.code:
class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, money):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = money
a = Account("Jieun", 5000)
b = Account("Minsu", 300)
print(a.owner, a.balance)
print(b.owner, b.balance)

cards.say: Objects can go in a list too. In a for loop, c is one object at a time, so print an attribute like c.name, not the object itself.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The moment Cat("Momo") is called, __init__ runs and "Momo" goes into self.name.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: a and b each have their own self.balance. 1000 plus 500 is 1500.

items.q: What happens when you run this code?
items.explain: __init__ is waiting for a name value, but Cat() gave it nothing. You get a clue (TypeError) saying a value is missing.

items.q: Fill in the blank so Jieun is printed.
items.explain: The object comes in through the first parameter, self. Here this and me were never set up as names (the parameter is called self), so they cause a NameError.

items.q: Put the lines in order so Jieun is printed.
items.explain: Write __init__ inside the blueprint first, then make the object. Only once it's made can you read a.owner.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: for takes the objects out one at a time as a. It adds 1000 and then 500, making 1500.

items.q: Fill in the blank so Nabi and Momo are printed in turn.
items.explain: c is one Cat object, and its name lives in the attribute name. It has no attribute c.cats or c.Cat, so those cause an AttributeError.

items.task: Read the owner's name and the balance, in that order, with input() (leave the parentheses empty; use int() for the balance). Make class Account whose __init__(self, owner, money) attaches self.owner and self.balance, make a with Account(…), and print. For Jieun, 5000: Jieun: 5000 won
hints: The name and balance change with each input. What should come out for Minsu and 0?
To take values when an object is made, use __init__. Attach the values it gets to self.
In __init__, put values into self.owner and self.balance. Call Account(…) with the two inputs to make a, then print a.owner and a.balance.
items.solution:
class Account:
    def __init__(self, owner, money):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = money
owner = input()
money = int(input())
a = Account(owner, money)
print(f"{a.owner}: {a.balance} won")
items.explain: __init__ attaches the values it gets to self, so the same blueprint works for any owner and balance. A balance of 0 is fine too.

items.q: In __init__(self, name), what is self?
options: The very object being made right now
items.explain: self is the very thing that's just being made. self.name = name means “attach name to this thing”.

LESSONS.title: Methods
LESSONS.goal: Write methods that give objects actions
summary: A def inside a class is a method
The first parameter is the object itself (always name it self)
Call object.method() to change attributes
Fill self.items = [] with a method

cards.say: A function made with def inside a class is called a method. It's an action the object can do. Call it with a dot, like a.deposit(500), and inside it, self changes that object's values.
Methods can hand back a value with return too. And you must always write self in the first spot, because when you call a.deposit(500), Python secretly passes a in as the first value.
You can put an empty list in an attribute and fill it one item at a time with a method. Start with self.items = [] in __init__, and add fills it with append.

items.q: What happens when you run this code?
items.explain: When you call d.bark(), Python secretly passes d as the first value. There's no spot (self) to take it, so you get a clue (TypeError) saying “takes 0 but 1 was given”. A method's first parameter receives the object itself, and by convention it's always named self.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Each call to up adds 1 to self.n. Called twice, it goes from 0 to 2.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The double method of the object made with Box(4) returns self.w * 2. Twice 4 is 8.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the deposit works.
items.explain: The first parameter is self. With this, the self below becomes a name that doesn't exist, so NameError, and using n again gives two parameters the same name, so SyntaxError.

items.q: Put the lines in order so wallet is printed.
items.explain: Write the method inside the blueprint, and call w.show() after making the object. Without an object, you can't call it.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: __init__ makes a separate empty list for each object. The bread went into a's list only, so b's list is empty: 0.

items.q: Fill in the blank so 2 is printed.
items.explain: The method that adds one item to a list is append. Lists have no method called add or items, so those cause an AttributeError.

items.task: Read the balance, a deposit and a withdrawal, in that order, with input() (leave the parentheses empty; use int()). Give Account(balance) the methods deposit and withdraw and call them with a dot. If the withdrawal is bigger than the balance, use if to print “Not enough money” and don't subtract. Finally print “Balance: N won”. For 1000, 500, 300: Balance: 1200 won
hints: The balance changes with the deposit, then the withdrawal. What happens if the withdrawal is exactly the balance?
A method is a def inside the class. Use its first parameter, self, to change the object's balance.
deposit increases balance. withdraw uses if to check whether the amount is bigger than balance: if so, print the message; otherwise, subtract.
items.explain: Withdrawing exactly the balance is an edge case, and it correctly gives 0 won. When there isn't enough, the balance isn't touched, so 1000 won stays.

items.q: When you write a method, what's the first parameter's name?
items.explain: A method's first parameter receives the object itself, and by convention it's always named self. In a.deposit(500), a comes in as self, so self.balance is a's value.

LESSONS.title: Inheritance
LESSONS.goal: Build a new class that inherits from a parent class
summary: class Dog(Pet): inherits what Pet has
A child can replace a method of the same name
super().__init__(…) lets the parent set up

cards.say: Write class Dog(Pet) and Dog inherits the Pet blueprint as it is. You can use d.hello() without writing hello again in Dog.

If the child has its own __init__, the parent's __init__ doesn't run by itself. Hand the setup to the parent with super().__init__(…). Then the parent takes care of name, and the child takes care of trick.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Dog inherits from Pet, so it can use hello. You don't need to write hello in Dog separately.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: When the child writes a method with the same name, the child's version is used first. The parent's hello is hidden, and only Woof woof is printed.

items.q: What happens when you run this code?
items.explain: Dog's __init__ hides Pet's __init__, so self.name was never made. You need to call super().__init__(name).

items.q: Fill in the blank so Dog inherits from Pet.
items.explain: Put the parent's name, Pet, in the parentheses. Lowercase pet is a name that doesn't exist, and Dog is still being built, so both cause a NameError.

items.q: Put the lines in order so Hello is printed.
items.explain: Pet has to be made first so Dog(Pet) can inherit from it. At the end, call hello on a Dog object.

items.task: Read a name and a trick, in that order, with input() (leave the parentheses empty). Make Pet (__init__(self, name), and info that prints “Name: …”) and Dog(Pet). Dog's __init__ uses super().__init__(name), and show prints self.info() and the trick. For Choco, shake: Name: Choco / Trick: shake (two lines)
hints: The two lines change with the name and trick you enter. The name is the parent's job, and the trick is the child's.
To hand the setup to the parent from the child's __init__, use super().__init__(…).
Pet stores name and prints it with info. Dog hands name over with super and stores trick, and show calls self.info() and then prints the trick.
items.explain: Printing the name uses the parent's info, inherited as it is. The child only adds its own trick, so nothing is repeated.

items.q: What does super().__init__(name) do?
options: It runs the parent class's __init__ for you
items.explain: The child's __init__ hides the parent's, so super() calls in the parent's setup work. No extra object is made.

LESSONS.title: Chapter 15 checkpoint
LESSONS.goal: Build a cafe ordering system with classes and inheritance
summary: A class is a blueprint; an object is the real thing
Attach attributes with __init__ and self; act with methods
class Child(Parent) inherits and replaces

cards.say: Let's wrap up Chapter 15. The Order blueprint gets a total and an add action, and Takeout inherits Order and changes only total. It's the skeleton of a cafe ordering system.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
class Cup:
    size = "large"
a = Cup()
b = Cup()
print(a.size, b.size)
items.explain: a and b made with Cup() are two objects from the same blueprint, so both have size large.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Call Cup("latte") and __init__ runs, putting latte into self.menu.

items.q: What happens when you run this code?
items.explain: c.fill() secretly passes c as the first value, but there's no spot (self) to take it. A method's first parameter receives the object itself, and by convention it's always named self.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: When the child writes a method with the same name again, the child's version is used. The parent's 4000 is hidden.

items.q: Fill in the blank so the parent's __init__ is called.
items.explain: super().__init__() hands the setup to the parent. self.__init__() calls itself again and repeats forever, and Order().__init__() sets up a different object, so self.sum never gets made.

items.task: Read the order type (dine-in or takeout) and two prices, in that order, with input() (leave the parentheses empty; int() for prices). Make Order (sum = 0 in __init__, add, total) and Takeout, which inherits it and adds 500 to total. Use if: Takeout() for takeout, otherwise Order(), then add twice. For takeout, 4500, 3000: Total: 8000 won
hints: Dine-in and takeout give different totals. What's the total for takeout when both prices are 0?
The child (Takeout) uses the parent (Order)'s add as it is and rewrites only total.
Use if on the order type to put Takeout() or Order() into o, then call add twice the same way and print total.
items.explain: add is inherited from the parent and only total changes, so nothing is repeated. A 0-won takeout correctly comes to 500 won, and dine-in comes out unchanged.

items.q: In Takeout(Order), how are Takeout and Order related?
items.explain: The one in the parentheses is the parent. Takeout is the child, so it can use Order's attributes and methods as they are.

ADVANCED.title: __str__ and __eq__
ADVANCED.goal: Decide how an object prints and when two books count as the same
summary: print shows the string __str__ returns
By default, == asks “is it the same thing?”
__eq__ decides “are the values equal?”

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. You don't need it to unlock the next chapter. In 15-2 you looped over objects in a list, right? Just print(b) gives hard-to-read text. Write __str__ and the string it returns gets printed.
By default, a == b asks “is it the same thing?”, so it's False even when the titles match. Write __eq__ and you decide what “equal values” means. in uses this rule too.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: print(c) prints the string __str__ returns. That string is “Cup: ” joined with self.size: Cup: large.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: Without __eq__, == only checks whether it's the same thing. a and b are two separately made objects, so it's False even with the same title.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: in compares each book in the list with ==. __eq__ compares titles, so the newly made Book("B") counts as being there: True.

items.q: Fill in after return so each book title prints on its own line.
items.explain: __str__ is a method that returns a string. Returning self.title does it. Putting print there returns None and causes a TypeError, and title is a name that doesn't exist.

items.q: Put the lines in order so Seat 7 is printed.
items.explain: Write __str__ inside the class first, then make the object s and print it. print(s) secretly calls __str__.

items.task: Give Book a __str__ (shaped like [title]) and an __eq__ (True when the titles match). Leave the code at the bottom (making two books, print, if) as it is. Two Moby Dicks: [Moby Dick]/[Moby Dick]/Same book
hints: The last line depends on whether the two titles match. Are Dune and dune, which differ only in capitals, the same book?
print(a) secretly calls __str__, and a == b secretly calls __eq__. Write both inside the class.
__str__ returns the title wrapped in square brackets, and __eq__ returns the result of comparing the two titles. Then if checks a == b.
items.explain: __str__ decided the printed shape, and __eq__ decided what counts as the same book. Only matching titles make the same book, so Dune and dune, differing only in capitals, are different books.

items.q: Without __eq__, what does a == b check?
options: Whether both names point to the same thing
Whether all attribute values of both objects match
Whether both classes have the same name
items.explain: By default it only checks whether it's the same thing. To compare attribute values, set that rule yourself in __eq__.

ADVANCED.title: Class attributes and collections
ADVANCED.goal: Work with values all objects share and with groups of objects
summary: Book.count is shared by every book
self.count = … is that object's own value
A manager object holding a list of objects

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. A value placed right under class, like kind in 15-1, is read by everyone. Change it through the class name and every object sees the new value.
cards.code:
class Book:
    count = 0
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title
        Book.count = Book.count + 1
a = Book("Moby Dick")
b = Book("Demian")
print(Book.count)
print(a.count, b.count)

cards.say: Here's a trap. Changing it with self.count = … doesn't touch the class value; it makes a new value on that object only. Like self.items = [] in 15-3, keep a collection in an attribute of a manager object.
cards.code:
class Book:
    count = 0
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title
        self.count = self.count + 1
a = Book("Moby Dick")
print(Book.count, a.count)

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
class Ticket:
    sold = 0
    def __init__(self, seat):
        self.seat = seat
        Ticket.sold = Ticket.sold + 1
a = Ticket(1)
b = Ticket(2)
c = Ticket(3)
print(Ticket.sold)
items.explain: Ticket.sold is one value shared by every ticket. It goes up by 1 each time a ticket is made, so after 3 tickets it's 3.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
class Ticket:
    sold = 0
    def __init__(self, seat):
        self.seat = seat
        self.sold = self.sold + 1
a = Ticket(1)
b = Ticket(2)
print(Ticket.sold, a.sold)
items.explain: self.sold = … doesn't change the class value; it gives each object its own sold. The class's sold stays 0, and a's sold is 1.

items.q: What's the output?
items.code:
class Cat:
    kind = "cat"
a = Cat()
b = Cat()
a.kind = "lion"
print(a.kind, b.kind, Cat.kind)
items.explain: a.kind = … gives a new kind to a only. b and the class still have cat. To change it for everyone, change Cat.kind.

items.q: Fill in the blank so making two tickets prints 2.
items.code:
class Ticket:
    sold = 0
    def __init__(self):
        Ticket.sold = ___ + 1
a = Ticket()
b = Ticket()
print(Ticket.sold)
items.explain: Read the class value, add 1, and put it back into the class value. With 0 it's always 1, and plain sold is a name that doesn't exist, so NameError.

items.q: Put the lines in order: add a book to the manager object and print the count, 1.
items.explain: Shelf is a manager object with an empty list as an attribute. Make the object, add with append, and count with len at the end.

items.task: Read the number of books n, then n titles one per line, with input() (leave the parentheses empty). Each time a Book is made, raise Book.count by 1 in __init__ and put the book in Shelf's books. The “Books: N” line is in the starter. After it, print the titles one per line. For 2 books: Books: 2/Moby Dick/Demian
items.starter:
class Book:
    count = 0
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title
        # raise Book.count by 1 here
class Shelf:
    def __init__(self):
        self.books = []
n = int(input())
shelf = Shelf()
# make n books here and
# put them in shelf.books
print("Books: " + str(Book.count))
# then the titles, one per line
hints: The output changes with the number of books. Whether it's 1 book or 3, the “Books: N” line prints after all the books are made.
Each time a book is made, raise the shared count with Book.count, and append the book to Shelf's list.
Raise Book.count in __init__. In a loop, read input() to make a Book and put it in shelf.books, and at the end print Book.count and the titles.

Book.count = Book.count + 1  (in Book's __init__)
shelf = Shelf()
for i in range(n):
    shelf.books.append(Book(___))
items.explain: Book.count goes up with every book made, and the books themselves gather in Shelf's list. The count is printed after all the books are made, so Books: N is right.

items.q: What's the difference between Book.count = Book.count + 1 and self.count = self.count + 1?
options: First: shared by all; second: a new value on that object only
items.explain: Changing it through the class name changes the value every object sees. Changing it through self makes a new attribute on that object only.

ADVANCED.title: Library lending system
ADVANCED.goal: Handle borrowing and returning with Book and Library
summary: A method returns True/False
Library manages a collection of books
if lib.borrow(…): checks for success

cards.say: This is where we go one step further. A method can return True or False too. Return whether it worked, and the caller uses that value to decide what to do next.

Library is a manager object that holds a collection of books. It finds a book by title and returns True if it lends it, or False if the book is missing or already out. The caller sorts it out with if.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: The first lend() marks the book as out. The second lend() finds it already out and returns False, and that gets printed.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: A method without return gives back no value, so None is printed. To use the result, hand it back, like return True.

items.q: What's the output?
items.explain: return False is inside the for, so it ends with False as soon as the first book, A, differs from B. To return False after checking them all, put it outside the for.

items.q: Fill in after return so the titles of books on loan are printed.
items.explain: print(b) prints the text __str__ returns. You must return self.title to get the title; the others cause errors.

items.q: Put the lines in order so it lends a book and prints Success.
items.explain: Make the method, then the object, and check the True that borrow() returns with if. Indent print under the if.

items.task: The Library has Dune, Demian and Hamlet. Read the command count n, then “borrow title” or “return title” lines with input(). borrow and give_back return True/False; print “Borrow OK” or “Borrow failed” (and “Return OK” or “Return failed”). At the end print “On loan: N” and those books with print(b)

return Dune

Return OK

return Demian

hints: A borrowed book can't be borrowed again. Returning or borrowing a book that isn't there fails too. The final list follows shelf order.
borrow finds a book with the same title that isn't out, sets out to True and returns True. If nothing is found, it returns False outside the for.
give_back does the reverse: it finds a book that's out and sets out to False. In the loop, use split to separate the command from the title, then call one of the two methods with if.
items.explain: borrow and give_back report whether they worked, so the caller picks the message with a single if. A missing book, borrowing twice and returning twice are all caught as False.

items.q: When borrow returns True/False, which form checks for success?
items.explain: Calling the method with parentheses makes the returned True/False the condition. lib.borrow without parentheses is the method itself, so it always counts as true.

TEMPLATES.explain: The value stored in self.name in __init__ comes out with p.name. The age is kept separately in p.age. → {OUT}
The method changes self.n, the value inside the object. Call add twice and it adds twice. Leave out self and it causes an error. → {OUT}

TEMPLATES.q: Fill in the blank so the “{NAME}” object takes and stores a name when it's made.
TEMPLATES.explain: The method called automatically when an object is made is named __init__. Methods with other names aren't called automatically.
When a child class rewrites a method with the same name, the child's version is used first. Make it with Pet and the parent's version runs. → {OUT}

TEMPLATES.q: Fill in the blank so the parent's __init__ is called to store the name.
TEMPLATES.explain: super() means the parent class. super().__init__(name) calls the parent's __init__ to store the name. The other names don't exist in the parent, so they cause an error.
